title: How Police Lineups Work
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open with a plug-heavy intro (Ben and Noel's Ridiculous History, merch, a listener suggestion from Britney Shift) and then explore police lineups: why eyewitness testimony is unreliable, the Jerry Miller wrongful conviction, simultaneous vs. sequential and double-blind lineup procedures, the disputed Illinois pilot study, filler recruitment (including Robert Weston), show-ups, and cross-race identification. They close with a listener email from Sarah Strantz about her baby calming down to the podcast.

segments.title: Opening banter and Ridiculous History plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome guests Ben and Noel, who talk about their show Ridiculous History, including the St. Louis racist Olympics anecdote, and plug merchandise and listener channels.

segments.title: Listener suggestion and the Jerry Miller case
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the police lineup topic from listener Britney Shift and a National Institute of Justice article. They describe Jerry Miller, convicted on two eyewitness identifications, who served twenty-four years before DNA exonerated him through the Innocence Project.

segments.title: Why eyewitness memory is unreliable
segments.summary: The hosts explain that human memory and perception are poor recorders, citing stress, adrenaline, and weapon focus. Chuck shares his own experience failing to identify suspects in a hit-and-run, and they discuss cross-race identification difficulty.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before the lineup fundamentals segment.

segments.title: Simultaneous vs. sequential lineups and double-blind administration
segments.summary: The hosts describe simultaneous and sequential lineup formats, relative vs. absolute judgment, and double-blind administration, noting how administrator cues can mislead witnesses. They discuss telling witnesses the suspect may not be present.

segments.title: Illinois pilot study and its flawed methodology
segments.summary: They discuss a Illinois multi-year study that appeared to favor simultaneous non-blind lineups, why its methodology was criticized, and police resistance to blind administrators, with the idea of a dedicated administrator.

segments.title: Building fair lineups, fillers, and Robert Weston
segments.summary: The hosts explain one suspect per lineup, matching fillers to the suspect or the witness description, dressing fillers alike, and the use of paid fillers recruited by casting agent Robert Weston in New York.

segments.title: Show-ups, investigatory vs. confirmatory lineups, and memory contamination
segments.summary: They describe show-ups as the worst format, how seeing a suspect in custody contaminates memory, and the difference between investigatory and confirmatory lineups.

segments.title: Listener mail: baby calmed by the podcast
segments.summary: Sarah Strantz writes that her crying baby calmed down when the show came on in the car. The hosts read the email and mention how to contact the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up, mention social media and email contact, and sign off.
